summary: This program is the farmers' market report from earlier in the chapter, now updated so that the vendor list comes back alphabetically with duplicates removed, and so that a vendor's menu shows at most three items. Each report is a separate static method holding one stream pipeline.

lines.text: Comparator supplies the ready-made comparison objects that sorted() needs when you want to order by something other than a value's natural order, such as by price.
Every report below reads from this one list, so the streams have a single source of data.
Calling a named method instead of writing the pipeline inline keeps main readable and lets you test each report on its own.
The method name still says "Set", but it now returns a List because a list can hold a guaranteed order while a plain set cannot.
Storing the vendor name in a variable means the menu lookup and the discount calculation below cannot drift apart.
forEach with a method reference prints each menu line on its own row, which reads better than printing the whole list in brackets.
This call points at step 3, which is still only a comment at the bottom of the class, so you must write that method before the file will compile.
The null check on getSeason() comes before the call to toLowerCase(), which is what stops a missing season from crashing the pipeline.
comparingDouble reads the price out of each product and orders the stream from cheapest to most expensive.
Sorting happens while the elements are still products, so mapping to names afterwards keeps the price order in the finished list of strings.
A stream can only be walked once, so collect gathers the results into a list you can print, return, and reuse.
This turns a stream of products into a stream of vendor names, which is all the rest of this pipeline needs.
Filtering out null and blank vendors keeps empty entries from showing up in the printed list and from breaking the sort.
Many products share a vendor, so distinct() keeps only the first occurrence of each name.
With no comparator, sorted() uses the natural order of the elements, which for strings is alphabetical — this is the first change the reader asked for.
equalsIgnoreCase matches the vendor whatever the capitalization, and the two null checks guard both sides of the comparison.
This line is commented out on purpose: with it enabled the menu would list items alphabetically, so it is worth switching on to see how it changes which three items survive the limit.
String.format with %.2f pins each price to two decimal places so the menu lines up like real money.
limit stops the stream after three elements, which is the second requested change; because it comes after map, it counts finished menu lines.
